title: At SC26, IBM accelerates progress in bringing quantum & HPC together
content: Quantum Research Blog At SC26, IBM accelerates progress in bringing quantum & HPC together At SC26 in Chicago, IBM and partners show how quantum computers are integrating into workflows and tools that the supercomputing workforce already runs. Date 16 Nov 2026 Authors Rafi Letzter Topics Error Correction & Mitigation Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key Takeaways: IBM and NVIDIA are integrating the open-source Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) with Slurm’s Hierarchical Resources (HRES) feature to give Slurm, the high-performance computing (HPC) workload manager NVIDIA develops, more visibility into quantum resources and workloads. IBM, RIKEN, and NVIDIA researchers used ROQUO, RIKEN's new GPU supercomputer, to bring an SQD calculation of an iron–sulfur cluster within 4.3 millihartree of DMRG, a classical method known for its high accuracy, 79× closer than earlier SQD work. IBM and NVIDIA, together with Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab), will launch a modular quantum computing co-design platform to explore computationally demanding problems in high-energy and nuclear physics. IBM and AMD announced Pelagos, an open-source framework that tests quantum error correction decoders against billions of simulated error patterns on GPUs. Managed workflows help researchers deploy, reuse, and run quantum-classical workflows on managed, high-performance classical infrastructure. Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM are finalists for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize for simulating protein-ligand complexes of up to 12,635 atoms with quantum and classical computers working together. IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 runs up to 100,000 samples per second, a 25× throughput gain over IBM Quantum Heron. Researchers can start on IBM quantum computers today with the free IBM Quantum Open Plan. This year, IBM and partners demonstrated quantum advantage . The next job is making quantum computers practical tools for science. We are on that path, which runs through high-performance computing (HPC) centers. In an HPC-plus-quantum paradigm , quantum processors, CPUs, and GPUs work together, with each compute tool managing the part of a problem it handles best. But maturing these integrations requires software that fits into existing HPC workflows, integrating highly performant quantum hardware with classical HPC, and access for the researchers who will use them. IBM and partners are bringing new progress on each of these fronts to SC26 , the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage, and Analysis, November 15–20 in Chicago. In particular, we are unveiling new open-source tools that support QPU-GPU integrations across classical hardware vendors, and working with AMD and NVIDIA on software and platforms that bring together advanced classical and quantum hardware for quantum error correction. Integrating quantum computing and HPC Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM are finalists for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize for outstanding achievement in supercomputing. They earned the spot by simulating protein-ligand complexes of up to 12,635 atoms , the largest molecules known to be simulated with quantum computers. This work is an example of quantum-HPC integration. Classical computers broke each complex into clusters and solved the simpler, less entangled ones. To solve the more complex and entangled clusters, the workflow used IBM Quantum Heron processors at Cleveland Clinic and RIKEN alongside classical HPC as part of a method called sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). The team has since automated the workflow using ROQUO, RIKEN’s new supercomputer built on NVIDIA GB200 NVL4 systems. ROQUO also powers new research from IBM, RIKEN, and NVIDIA. The team used SQD to study Fe₄S₄, an iron–sulfur cluster found inside the proteins of living cells. Its strongly interacting electrons make it hard to simulate. The researchers started SQD from a broken-symmetry reference state, a starting approximation that better captures the magnetic interactions between the cluster's iron atoms. The results came within 4.3 millihartree of the accuracy achieved with the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG), a classical simulation method known for its high accuracy. That's 79× closer than the team's earlier closed-loop SQD result on the same cluster. In Illinois, a team from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (U of I.), the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA), and IBM connected NCSA's DeltaAI supercomputer to an IBM quantum computer. Within six months of expanding their collaboration in April , they used the combined system to model Cu₃C₆O₆, a strongly correlated kagome-lattice metal. Its structure forms a pattern of corner-sharing triangles, and its electrons interact too strongly for standard approximations to describe. The team will present the results at SC26.
